comparison: Both evaluate competitive repopulation experiments (C28-C31). OpenEval finds the data consistently demonstrate age-dependent functional decline of miR-146a KO HSCs with appropriate controls. Peer reviewers question the data presentation and interpretation, requesting absolute cell counts to clarify whether depletion is cell-autonomous or indirect.

Both address proliferation data after chronic LPS and the relationship between NF-κB activation and proliferation (C43, C44, C67, C68). OpenEval finds the BrdU/Ki-67 data support a non-cell-autonomous mechanism. Peer reviewers request additional experiments to directly test NF-κB+ versus NF-κB− fractions and note missing no-LPS controls limit interpretation.

Both evaluate human MDS data showing reduced miR-146a (C53, C54, C87). OpenEval expresses uncertainty due to missing sample details and questions about causal involvement. Peer reviewers accept this observational finding without raising concerns, viewing it as supporting evidence for disease relevance.

Both evaluate NF-κB reporter data and genetic rescue experiments (C38-C42, plus C7 in OpenEval). OpenEval finds strong support from p50 deletion rescue experiments. Peer reviewers acknowledge the data but note it provides only indirect evidence and request additional experiments to test cell-autonomous NF-κB action.

Both evaluate LPS acceleration experiments (C25, C26, C27). OpenEval finds the core findings about chronic inflammation well-supported, though notes C27 involves speculation. Peer reviewers identify missing no-LPS controls as undermining interpretation of the results.

Both evaluate longitudinal FACS data showing age-dependent HSC changes (C2-C5, C19-C24). OpenEval finds comprehensive support across multiple time points. Peer reviewers question whether HSCs are truly depleted versus mobilized to spleen, requesting total HSC counts across both compartments and questioning the 'accelerated differentiation' interpretation.

Both evaluate the proposed mechanistic model (C57-C60, plus C72 in OpenEval and C61 in peer review). OpenEval finds the model well-supported by multiple lines of evidence including TRAF6, NF-κB, and IL-6 data. Peer reviewers explicitly criticize the model as 'highly speculative,' emphasizing the distinction between tested claims and speculation.

Both evaluate reciprocal transplant experiments addressing cell-autonomous versus environmental effects (C6, C32-C35, plus C62-C64 in peer review). OpenEval finds clear support for HSC-intrinsic effects with modest environmental contribution. Peer reviewers question whether miR-146a acts cell-autonomously in HSCs and suggest additional experiments to directly test this.

Both evaluate Rag1 knockout experiments showing lymphocyte contribution (C36, C37, plus C48 and C63 in OpenEval). Both agree this demonstrates lymphocyte involvement in the phenotype, though peer reviewers use this finding to raise questions about the relative importance of intrinsic versus extrinsic effects.

Both evaluate IL-6 mechanism data (C45-C47, C69, plus C48-C49, C70, C73 in peer review). OpenEval finds support from RT-qPCR, genetic rescue, and in vitro experiments showing IL-6 as an important but not sole mediator. Peer reviewers raise fundamental questions about which cells secrete IL-6, whether it acts on HSCs versus other cells, and whether it promotes differentiation versus progenitor proliferation.

Both evaluate TRAF6 data and its role in the mechanism (C50, C51, C65, plus C52, C66 in OpenEval and C7 in peer review). OpenEval finds support from RT-qPCR and overexpression experiments, noting the overexpression may be more severe than endogenous derepression. Peer reviewers question whether the modest TRAF6 increase mediates effects, whether it acts autonomously in HSCs, and whether other TRAF6-regulated pathways beyond NF-κB/IL-6 are important.

Partial overlap on IL-6 mechanism. OpenEval R11 evaluates in vitro IL-6 stimulation experiments (C49, C70, C73) showing effects on LSK cells but not long-term HSCs. Peer R9 addresses broader IL-6 mechanism questions including which cells secrete IL-6 and whether it acts on HSCs versus other cells.

Partial overlap on TRAF6 overexpression experiments. OpenEval R13 evaluates transplant experiments with TRAF6-overexpressing cells (C52, C66) showing severe phenotypes. Peer R10 questions whether modest TRAF6 increases mediate effects and whether TRAF6 acts autonomously, expressing skepticism about the overall model.

Minimal overlap. OpenEval R17 synthesizes evidence for multi-cellular contributions (C62, C64, C71). Peer R5 questions cell-autonomous versus non-autonomous effects based on competitive repopulation and Rag rescue data, requesting additional experiments.

Minimal overlap on C27 (environmental bacterial exposure). Both express uncertainty: OpenEval notes this is reasonable speculation not directly tested; peer reviewers note missing no-LPS controls undermine interpretation of inflammation experiments.

Minimal overlap on C24 (increased splenic HSPCs). OpenEval R3 includes this as part of comprehensive longitudinal data. Peer R2 accepts this finding and uses it to raise questions about HSC mobilization versus depletion.

OpenEval evaluates background on miR-146a function and knockout model characterization (C1, C14, C15). No corresponding peer review evaluation found; reviewers focused on experimental claims rather than established background.

OpenEval evaluates RT-qPCR and FACS data showing expression patterns and normal hematopoiesis in young mice (C16-C18). No corresponding peer review evaluation found; reviewers focused on age-dependent phenotypes rather than baseline characterization.

OpenEval evaluates progression to bone marrow failure/tumors and epidemiological associations (C9, C85). No corresponding peer review evaluation found; reviewers focused on mechanistic claims rather than disease progression.

OpenEval evaluates background knowledge and prior work (C10-C13, C74-C86). No corresponding peer review evaluation found; these represent established context rather than claims requiring experimental validation in the current study.
